paper.title: Measurement of Electromagnetic Feedthrough in Spin Wave Based Microwave Multiport Devices
paper.abstract: Multiport radio-frequency (RF) input devices are designed to handle multiple signals simultaneously. These devices typically consist of multiple input ports that can receive different RF signals and combine them into a single output or distribute them to multiple outputs. For example, in wave computing, majority gates use an odd number of inputs and one output. This paper investigates the electromagnetic feedthrough of a 3-input/1-output majority gate layout based on spin waves (SWMGs) and U-shaped microwave spin-wave transducers. The paper addresses the challenges of electromagnetic feedthrough by exploring shielding techniques to understand and improve the performance of the SWMG. As a tradeoff in complexity and performance, the unshielded layout is optimized and fabricated on a 500 nm Yttrium Iron Garnet (YIG) film. Measurements of scattering (S-) parameters demonstrate spin wave propagation at 8 GHz for a 200 mT magnetic bias field, with reduced electromagnetic coupling. Furthermore, the study includes an analysis of the effective permittivity and loss tangent of Gadolinium Gallium Garnet (GGG) substrate, critical for accurate electromagnetic modeling of the device.

## Citation Analysis

Self-citations counted by author-name overlap: [5] (Adelmann, Ciubotaru), [7] (roadmap with Adelmann, Ciubotaru among ~100 authors), [8], [9], [10] (Ciubotaru, Meng, Adelmann), [11], [12], [21] (all six authors, CAS 2024), [23], [24]. SCR = 10/26 = 38.5%. Every self-citation concerns spin-wave computing, majority gates or inductive transducers, so topical similarity is high (>=0.5) throughout; the problem is the share, not the relevance. The pattern reflects a co-author group (IMEC) that is central to this sub-field, but the rule is applied as specified. Minor bibliographic defects: [6] carries a LaTeX artefact ("textbf109(8)"), [25] has a malformed DOI link and [26] a doubled scheme ("http://https://").

---

## Structural Analysis

Claims are tied to measured S-parameter plots (Figs. 8, 12) and an EM simulation (Fig. 9); the claim-evidence balance is adequate. Limitations are acknowledged inline: the GGG model agrees with measurement "up to 18 GHz and the model for the GGG material parameters needs improvements for higher frequencies", and the risk of parasitic spin waves from shield currents is discussed. Several weaknesses: Sections 2 and 3 largely restate the authors' CAS 2024 paper [21] (the GGG extraction is attributed to [21] and the shielding result is said to be "in agreement with those presented in [21]"), and the page carrying Fig. 8 reproduces a conference footer ("CAS 2024 International Semiconductor Conference, Oct. 9 - 11, 2024, Sinaia, Romania"), suggesting a figure taken from a presentation. The claimed "clear improvement of up to 10 dB" compares the YIG device near 7.3 GHz with the earlier GGG-only test structures, so the effect of the tapered contacts is confounded with substrate and frequency. The conclusion's feedthrough range (-37...-47 dB) does not exactly match the body (-36, -42, -48 dB). No measurement data, layouts or simulation models are released; the artifact category is none.

---

## Conclusion

A competent experimental device paper whose few equations are necessary and whose results are supported by measurement. It is weakened by heavy overlap with the authors' own conference paper and a confounded headline comparison. Under the specification it is disqualified by an excessive self-citation ratio (38.5%), even though each self-citation is relevant; readers should weigh that flag as a share-of-references signal from a dominant research group rather than citation padding.

paper.title: Impact of Scaling and Interface Roughness on Drain Current in Nanosheet and Nanowire FETs: A 3D Monte Carlo Analysis
paper.abstract: A 3D finite-element Monte Carlo simulation toolbox, incorporating Schrödinger equation-based quantum corrections, is employed to analyze the performance of nanosheet (NS) and nanowire (NW) field-effect transistors (FETs), which emerged as promising candidates for sub-3 nm CMOS technology. The study investigates the impact of scaling gate length and oxide thickness, increase in source/drain doping concentration, and interface roughness on these architectures. Results indicate that NS-FETs achieve higher ON currents than NW FETs. However, scaling the gate length below 12 nm reduces the drain current in both devices with a ⟨110⟩ channel orientation—by 9.4% in NS and 7.7% in NW. To understand this decline, valley population and average electron velocity are examined. Scaling dielectric thickness has a smaller effect on NW-FETs with 12 nm and 10 nm gate lengths compared to NS-FETs. In contrast, changes in maximum doping concentration have a greater impact on NW than NS, due to better electrostatic control and increased carrier injection resulting from reduced source/drain resistance. A back-scattering effect is observed in the 12 nm and 10 nm gate length devices, particularly NWs, but it can be mitigated by increasing doping concentration. Interface roughness significantly degrades drain current (IDD), with a more pronounced impact on NWs. Their smaller surface-to-volume ratio and stronger quantum confinement increase sensitivity to roughness variations, as most carriers are closer to the surface, leading to more scattering events. On the contrary, NSs, despite interface roughness, benefit from a larger conductive cross-section, maintaining higher effective mobility in the device channel.

A clearly reported simulation study with appropriate (essentially absent) formalism and a credible validation step, but a modest conceptual contribution beyond the authors' prior work and several abstract-conclusion inconsistencies. paper.title: Design Space Exploration of Current-Starved Ring Oscillators Based on Graphene Nanoribbons
paper.abstract: Graphene is well-suited for ultra-low-power (ULP) nano-electronics due to its exceptional characteristics like ballistic transport and its ability to engineer structures featuring a geometry-induced bandgap. Identifying the conditions necessary for achieving the maximum level of performance and of power-efficiency frequently requires a design space exploration (DSE). By means of calibration and external regulation of the supply voltage, the ULP graphene-nanoribbon (GNR) ring oscillator presented in this paper is capable of exceeding the performance of its 7 nm FinFET counterpart both in terms of maximum frequency and of power-efficiency. Under nominal supply voltage conditions we achieve a 1.89× higher output frequency while simultaneously reducing the power consumption by 553.8× and achieving a 812× higher power efficiency. After performing a DSE and leveraging both externally-applied supply voltage modulation and output frequency calibration we achieved a 4.81× higher maximum output frequency operation mode and a 242× higher maximum power-efficiency operation mode when configuring both blocks for peak performance for each mode.

Notational errors rather than theater: the quantum capacitance is labelled "Cins" in the sentence introducing it, and the equivalent permittivity is written "µeq". The parallel-plate capacitance equation is described but not shown.

[6], [8], [9] are cited together as examples of GNR synapses and neurons, a marginal relation. Bibliographic errors: Dirac's 1928 paper [15] is given as "Physical Review 117(778)" (it appeared in Proc. R. Soc. A), and [17] carries the placeholder "year, 2007".

Results are simulation-only and presented in Figs. 5-7 and Tables 2-4; the claim-evidence balance is adequate. The headline ratios select endpoints inconsistently: 1.89x (88.4/46.7 GHz) and 553.8x (321.2/0.58 µW) use the upper ends of the ranges in Table 2, while 812x (113.7/0.14 GHz/µW) uses the lower ends; the upper-end efficiency ratio is about 376x. Design drawbacks are acknowledged inline (quiescent current of the current DAC, the "pronounced non-linear characteristic" of frequency versus DAC code), but process variation, temperature and GNR fabrication feasibility are not evaluated. The co-simulation framework and GNR models are not released; the only link is to third-party MATLAB codes, which do not count. Artifact category: none.

---

A modest incremental design study, an extension of the authors' conference paper, with appropriate and necessary formalism. Its main weaknesses are optimistic and inconsistently derived headline figures, the absence of variability analysis for a single-ended oscillator, and an elevated self-citation share; it carries a medium-severity flag only.

paper.title: An Area-Optimized Digitally-Assisted DAC Employing a Matrix-Based DEM Scheme
paper.abstract: The Dynamic Element Matching (DEM) technique’s role is to mitigate mismatch issues in complex, matrix-based systems. Previous work employing a matrix-based random DEM scheme demonstrated enhanced linearity and spectral characteristics in the Digital to Analog Converter’s (DAC) thermometric decoded section. This paper presents the design of an area-optimized, DEM-assisted 9-bit segmented DAC. The optimal segmentation level for area-performance is initially established. Subsequently, to mitigate area constraints from the integral nonlinearity (INL) requirement and improve spectral performance, we utilize the matrix-based DEM engine from prior research. The proposed 9-bit DAC, implemented in a commercial 180 nm CMOS process, achieves a total harmonic distortion (THD) of -79 dB and a spurious-free dynamic range (SFDR) of 79 dB, resulting in 8× and 16× improvements in SFDR and THD, respectively, over its non-DEM counterpart.

**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** Both the segmentation methodology ([2]) and the DEM engine ([6]) are existing; the paper applies them to a specific design point. This is a standard design methodology applied to a new instance, Level 2.

**Assessment:** Proportionate. The area and DNL/INL equations are standard and are actually used to generate the segmentation trade-off in Fig. 5, so they pass the necessity test. Equations (12)-(14) are expository (the average of two mismatched elements); they could be said in a sentence but are basic equations of the kind tolerated at Level 2, not one of the theater patterns.

### Issues
Cross-references are broken: "as shown in 2.1.3.." and "as predicted by 2.1.3.." point to a section number where an equation is meant, and "According to (), DNL spikes appear" has an empty reference. Section 2.1.3 cites Fig. 3a for the DNL curves (they are in Fig. 3b) and says 100 DACs while the caption says 30.

Self-citations: [1] (Dumitru, Ilie, Enachescu), [5] (Calinescu, Enachescu), [6] (Calinescu, Antonovici, Enachescu); SCR = 3/13 = 23.1%. All three are on DACs or DEM and are relevant; [6] is the immediate predecessor whose engine is reused. The reference list is short (13 items) for a DAC design paper, which magnifies the ratio.

---

## Structural Analysis

The MATLAB predictions are checked against MC simulations, and the DEM ON/OFF comparison is quantified in Table 1, so claim-evidence balance is adequate for the core result. However, all results are simulations, while the abstract's "implemented in a commercial 180 nm CMOS process, achieves" reads as a silicon result. The "8x and 16x" improvements are power ratios of the 9 dB and 12 dB gains in Table 1. Several figures do not reconcile: the conclusions give 3.14 mA at 1.8 V, but the reported controller (3.42 mW) and current sources (184 µW) imply about 2 mA; the stated active area of 12999 µm2 differs from the sum of the reported parts (7466 + 3469 + 1908 = 12843 µm2); the maximum DNL/INL of 0.75/0.57 LSB in the conclusions does not appear in the results. Section 3 specifies cells switching at 1.6 MHz, but Section 4.3 states the DEM engine limits the DAC to 1.56 MHz and the spectral test runs at 1 MHz. Constraints are acknowledged only inline (the 1.56 MHz limit, the passive-area overhead). No RTL, MATLAB scripts or simulation data are released; artifact category none.

---

## Conclusion

A small incremental design paper whose equations are standard and largely necessary, but whose presentation is careless: broken equation references, figure and count mismatches, and summary numbers that do not follow from the reported components. Self-citation is elevated, and the result is simulation-only though framed as an implementation.

paper.title: GaN Bootstrapped Logic Gates Analytical Modeling and Design Insights
paper.abstract: Following recent advancements, Gallium Nitride (GaN) technology continues to garner interest as a promising solution for future power electronics applications. Due to the variety of devices available in a monolithic GaN process, the development of digital circuits requires different topologies compared to CMOS technologies. This paper presents the analysis and design of logic gates from the bootstrapped family. Analytical equations for the static and dynamic parameters of an inverter are introduced. When compared to simulation results, these equations achieve a maximum error of 23.9% for static parameters and 33.3% for dynamic parameters. Additionally, different implementation details, such as developing other logic functions or enhancing the circuit behavior at system level, are proposed.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text; the SPICE testbenches and the "Verilog-A-based device model" are not released

verdict.summary: First-order analytical design equations for a GaN bootstrapped inverter, checked against SPICE across twelve sizings; the equations are the contribution and are proportionate, self-citation is low (1/24), and results are well tabulated, though derivations are mostly omitted and nothing is released.

## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Hand-analysis design equations for the bootstrapped GaN HEMT inverter: static equations (sizing, logic levels, power) carried over from the authors' CAS 2024 paper, plus new rise/fall time and propagation-delay approximations derived with a linear load-current assumption, validated against SPICE simulations of twelve inverter sizings in a 200 V GaN process.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** The equations are first-order square-law hand calculations obtained by the textbook method of Hodges et al. applied to a known topology (the bootstrapped inverter from a patent). This is an established analysis method applied to a new circuit; by the default-to-lower rule it is Level 2 rather than a new mathematical model at Level 3.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 (with constraints: 0)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 15 (bootstrap capacitor sizing (1)-(2), sizing ratio (3), logic levels (4)-(7), power (8), timing (9)-(13), minimum input frequency (14), percentage error (15))

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. The design equations are the contribution and are evaluated numerically against simulation in Table 2; a designer would use them to size devices. Eq. (2) is a rule of thumb and Eq. (15) a percentage error, both trivial but not decorative.

### Issues
None in the sense of theater. Only the derivation of (9)-(10) is outlined; (11)-(13) are "similarly derived" without steps, so their particular coefficients (e.g. 1.5, 3 and 2 in (12)-(13)) cannot be checked from the paper. Eq. (14) for the minimum input frequency is not validated anywhere in the results.

---

## Citation Analysis

One self-citation, [13] (Medinceanu and Enachescu, CAS 2024), which supplies the static equations and measurement method; SCR = 1/24 = 4.2%, normal and relevant. One attribution error: the text says the HEMT's challenges and principles "were discussed in this previous work [12]", but [12] is a patent by de Rooij et al., not the authors' work (probably [13] was meant). Several references are press releases, a datasheet and patents, which is acceptable for the industrial context described.

---

## Structural Analysis

Claims are well supported: Table 2 sets theoretical against simulated values for every parameter and sizing, and the stated maxima (23.9% static, 33.3% dynamic) match the table. Limitations are acknowledged inline: the authors note that the VOL error "is considerable" but small in absolute terms, that the timing approximations give "values of the correct magnitude" rather than precise ones, that initial high transitions are slewed, and that the static-current reduction of [24] slows tR. Unacknowledged limits: validation is against simulation with a device model only (the Verilog-A model is mentioned first in the conclusions), not against silicon, and the low-frequency behaviour promised in the introduction is covered only by the untested Eq. (14). The description of fmax as "the mean of tPLH and tPHL" is imprecise; the tabulated values correspond to the reciprocal of that mean. Nothing is released; artifact category none.

---

## Conclusion

A modest but honest extension of the authors' conference paper: the formalism is the substance of the contribution, is checked systematically against simulation with transparently reported errors, and the citation profile is clean. It would be stronger with full derivations, validation of the fmin relation, and silicon or at least process-corner data. No flags are raised.
